items.readable_text:
Content:
Many quadratic equations have two solutions. However, it's also possible for a quadratic equation to have only one solution or no real solutions at all.

Content:
For example, consider the following quadratic equation:

Content:
[MATH: (3x-6)^2=0]

Content:
We can solve this equation using the square root method:

Content:
[MATH: (3x − 6)^{2}|= 0; sqrt((3x − 6)^{2})|= sqrt(0);|3x − 6||= 0]

Content:
Normally, at this stage, we would obtain two solutions by setting the inside of the absolute value equal to positive or negative [MATH: (\pm)] the right-hand side. However, in this case, the right-hand side is zero, and [MATH: +0] and [MATH: -0] are both just [MATH: 0.]

Content:
So, we have only one solution:

Content:
[MATH: |3x − 6||= 0; 3x − 6|= 0; 3x|= 6; x|= 2]
